topic: Linear Transformations and Matrices: The Geometry of Space Warping

outline.topic: Linear Transformations and Matrices: The Geometry of Space Warping

sections.title: Prerequisites: Vectors as Directions
sections.content: Briefly recap that a vector [x, y] is a movement from the origin. Visualize a 2D coordinate grid with a 'Hero' character (a small robot) standing at (1, 1). Explain that the grid is built on two unit vectors: i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1).
sections.example: If the robot moves 3 steps along i-hat and 2 steps along j-hat, it reaches (3, 2).

sections.title: What is a 'Linear' Transformation?
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a transformation as a 'function' that moves vectors to new positions. For it to be 'Linear', two rules must hold: 1. The origin must remain fixed. 2. Grid lines must remain parallel and evenly spaced after the transformation.
sections.example: Imagine the grid is a rubber sheet. Stretching it or rotating it is linear; bending it into a circle or sliding the center is not.

sections.title: The Secret: Tracking the Basis Vectors
sections.content: Show that to understand where *any* vector goes, we only need to track where i-hat and j-hat land. If we know the new coordinates of i-hat and j-hat, we can deduce the entire transformed grid.
sections.example: If i-hat moves to (0, 1) and j-hat moves to (-1, 0), the entire grid has rotated 90 degrees counter-clockwise.

sections.title: Matrices: The Coordinate Containers
sections.content: Introduce the Matrix as a shorthand way to store these two 'landing' coordinates. The first column is the new i-hat, and the second column is the new j-hat. Multiplying a vector [x, y] by this matrix is just a recipe for where that vector ends up.
sections.example: A matrix [ [3, 0], [0, 2] ] means i-hat is now 3 units long and j-hat is now 2 units tall. This is a 'Scaling' transformation.

sections.title: Application: Transforming 'Yoga Cat'
sections.content: Use a complex shape, like a 2D drawing of a 'Yoga Cat' made of many vectors. Apply a 'Shear' matrix [ [1, 1], [0, 1] ] to show how the cat leans over while its feet stay on the ground.
sections.example: The cat's head at (1, 2) moves to (1*1 + 1*2, 0*1 + 1*2) = (3, 2). The cat appears to be leaning forward to catch a mouse.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Recap that matrices are not just blocks of numbers; they are descriptions of geometric movement. Every matrix multiplication is a transformation of space.
sections.example: A 2x2 matrix is simply a 'map' telling the grid how to dance.

storyboard.title: Prerequisites: Vectors as Directions
lecture_lines: Imagine a vector as movement from the origin.
Our grid is built on i-hat and j-hat.
Move 3 along i-hat and 2 along j-hat.
animations: Create a 2D coordinate grid (#444444) and a yellow dot (#FFFF00) at (1,1) labeled 'Robot'.
Create a red vector (#FF0000) for i-hat and a green vector (#00FF00) for j-hat.
Animate the yellow dot moving 2 units in the positive x direction.
Animate the yellow dot moving 1 unit in the positive y direction.
Draw a white vector (#FFFFFF) from (0,0) to (3,2) and display label '[3, 2]'.

storyboard.title: What is a 'Linear' Transformation?
lecture_lines: Transformations move vectors to new positions in space.
The origin must stay fixed in its place.
Grid lines must remain parallel and evenly spaced.
animations: Show a 2D grid (#444444) with a white dot (#FFFFFF) at (0,0).
Animate the grid rotating by 30 degrees and scaling by 1.2.
Highlight parallel grid lines by changing their color to cyan (#00FFFF).
Apply a wavy distortion to the grid, then smoothly transition back to the linear state.
Keep the origin dot (#FFFFFF) fixed while the rest of the grid moves.

storyboard.title: The Secret: Tracking the Basis Vectors
lecture_lines: We only need to track i-hat and j-hat.
Their new positions determine the entire transformed grid.
If i-hat moves here and j-hat moves there...
...every other vector follows their lead perfectly.
Tracking basis vectors reveals the secret of space warping.
animations: Show the unit vectors i-hat (#FF0000) and j-hat (#00FF00) on a standard grid.
Rotate the entire grid 90 degrees counter-clockwise; i-hat moves to (0,1), j-hat to (-1,0).
Display text labels 'New i-hat: (0, 1)' and 'New j-hat: (-1, 0)' near the vectors.

storyboard.title: Matrices: The Coordinate Containers
lecture_lines: A matrix stores the landing spots of basis vectors.
Column one is i-hat’s new home in space.
Column two is where j-hat lands after transformation.
Matrix multiplication is just a recipe for movement.
It scales or rotates the grid based on coordinates.
animations: Display a 2x2 matrix with red brackets and columns for i-hat and j-hat.
Scale the grid by 3x horizontally and 2x vertically; update matrix to [[3, 0], [0, 2]].
Label column 1 as 'i-hat destination' and column 2 as 'j-hat destination'.

storyboard.title: Application: Transforming 'Yoga Cat'
lecture_lines: Let’s apply a shear matrix to our Yoga Cat.
Watch how the cat leans while feet stay planted.
Every point on the cat follows the matrix rule.
Coordinates shift based on the new grid orientation.
Space warps, and the cat stretches into a lean.
animations: Create a shape resembling a cat (#FF00FF) using a set of connected line segments.
Show the matrix [[1, 1], [0, 1]] in the corner of the screen.
Apply a shear transformation: the grid and the cat lean to the right.
Highlight a vertex at (1, 2) and move it to (3, 2) with a ghost trail.
Display the calculation '(1*1 + 1*2, 0*1 + 1*2) = (3, 2)' next to the point.

storyboard.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: Matrices are geometric maps, not just blocks of numbers.
Every multiplication is a dance of coordinate space.
Linear algebra lets us describe warping with simple grids.
animations: Animate a sequence of three transformations: rotation, scaling, and then shearing.
Display the text 'Matrices are Geometric Maps' in bright green (#00FF00).
Fade out the grid and shapes, leaving only a 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] in the center.
